title: HS Codes for Spices, Dehydrated and Spray Dried Powders from India
content_html:
An HS code is the number customs authorities use to classify goods. When you import spices, dehydrated vegetable powders, spray dried fruit powders or herbal powders from India, the HS code on the shipping documents affects the duty you pay, the import controls that apply and how quickly your shipment clears. This article explains how HS codes work, lists the codes shown on the Tradenest Naturals specification sheets for our main products, and explains why your customs broker must confirm the final classification in your country.

What Is an HS Code?

HS stands for Harmonized System, a product classification maintained by the World Customs Organization and used by most trading countries. The first six digits are shared internationally:

  • Chapter (2 digits): the broad group, for example 09 for coffee, tea and spices, or 07 for vegetables
  • Heading (4 digits): a narrower group, for example 0904 for pepper and capsicum
  • Subheading (6 digits): a specific product type, for example 0904.12 for crushed or ground pepper

Each country then adds its own digits to create national tariff lines. India uses 8-digit ITC-HS codes for exports. The United States uses a 10-digit Harmonized Tariff Schedule number, the UK uses a 10-digit commodity code, Canada uses a 10-digit customs tariff classification, and the European Union uses an 8-digit Combined Nomenclature code with further TARIC digits for import measures.

Why the Export Code and Import Code Can Differ

The HS code on an Indian shipping bill is the exporter's classification under Indian rules. Your import declaration uses your own country's tariff. The first six digits usually match, but the extra digits differ by country, and in some cases customs in the importing country may classify the product under a different heading altogether.

This matters most for processed powders. A plain dried vegetable or spice is usually straightforward. A spray dried fruit powder that contains a carrier, a seasoning blend, or a powder made from juice rather than whole fruit may be classified differently depending on its exact composition. That is why the specification sheet and an accurate product description are as important as the code itself.

Notes on Specific Product Groups

Spices (Chapter 09)

Ground spices such as coriander, turmeric, chilli and pepper generally sit in Chapter 09. The subheading often depends on whether the spice is whole, crushed or ground, so state the form clearly on your purchase order.

Dehydrated vegetables (Chapter 07 and others)

Dried vegetables, whole, cut, sliced, broken or in powder, generally fall under heading 0712. Potato flour and flakes are classified under heading 1105, and spray dried tomato powder made from tomato paste is usually treated as a tomato preparation under 2002.90.

Spray dried fruit and juice powders

This is the group where classification needs the most care. A powder made from fruit pulp, a powder made from juice, and a powder that includes a carrier may each be treated differently. Fruit powders are generally classified as fruit flour and powder under 1106.30, but a powder with a significant carrier or added sugar may move to 2106.90. Share the product composition from the specification sheet with your broker before the first shipment.

Herbal powders (Chapter 12 and 13)

Plant parts used in herbal products are often classified in heading 1211 or 1212, while extracts and plant juices fall under heading 1302. The intended use and your local rules may affect the final line, so confirm this before you import.

How to Avoid Classification Problems

  1. Ask the supplier for the specification sheet and the HS code they will use on export documents.
  2. Send both to your customs broker before you confirm the order.
  3. Agree a clear product description that appears the same way on the invoice, packing list and certificate of origin.
  4. Check whether your country applies extra controls, quotas or trade measures to that tariff line.
  5. For regular imports, ask your broker whether a binding tariff ruling or advance ruling is worth applying for.

Classification rules and tariff rates change. Always confirm current requirements with your customs broker or the relevant authority, such as US Customs and Border Protection and the US FDA, HMRC and port health in the UK, the CBSA and CFIA in Canada, or the customs authority of your EU member state.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use the HS code from the supplier on my import declaration?

You can use it as a starting point, but the importer is responsible for classification in the importing country. Your national tariff extends the 6-digit code, and your broker should confirm the full line.

Why does the table show 6-digit codes?

The first six digits are the international HS subheading and are the same in every member country. National tariff lines add two to four more digits, and these differ between India, the USA, the UK and Canada. Your customs broker adds the correct national digits for your shipment.

Does the HS code affect import duty?

Yes. Duty rates, and any preferential rates, are set at the tariff-line level in each country. Your broker can tell you the current rate for your line.

Do you provide export documents with the HS code?

Yes. Tradenest Naturals is an IEC registered exporter and provides export documentation support. A product specification sheet is shared with every quotation.

What is the minimum order quantity?

The MOQ is 5 Kg per product. Samples are available on request, so you can review the product and specification sheet with your broker before ordering.
